quotes.text: Passing tests aren't evidence that your app will work across distributed services. They only confirm that internal logic works when fed controlled inputs.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the key limit of unit tests plainly.

quotes.text: But skipping them is dangerous because environment specific issues like mismatched que names or incorrect connection strings are exactly the kinds of failures that unit tests never see.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why integration tests cannot be skipped.

quotes.text: This approach eliminates the assumption that if the API says success, the job is done. It checks whether users get the actual success states promised to them.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Captures the unique value of browser-based front-end tests.

quotes.text: Each stage adds a different checkpoint, so errors are caught in the cheapest and earliest place possible before anyone has to debug them.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarizes the logic of a layered test pipeline.

quotes.text: Testing isn't about filling a checklist or keeping dashboards green. It's about building confidence that your app behaves the way you expect once it leaves your hands.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A clear statement of what testing is really for.

takeaways: Unit tests are fast and cheap for validating isolated logic, but they cannot catch serialization, configuration or cross-service failures.
Integration tests against real queues, databases and bindings expose environment issues such as mismatched queue names or broken connection strings.
Front-end tests with Playwright confirm what users actually see, and an Azure DevOps pipeline should run each layer at the stage where it is cheapest.
hook: A one-line change passes every unit test and still breaks orders, notifications and pages in production. This episode is for developers and DevOps teams building Azure apps who want to know which bugs unit, integration and front-end tests each catch, and how to orchestrate all three in one pipeline.
